name: Karl Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach guitar on Mondays, record short demo loops for other acts, and lead my band at Thursday rehearsal or a club show. My music master’s taught me to hear the whole arrangement; loading amps taught me to check the van first.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what bothers you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like watching a beginner land a clean chord and a room sing back. I dislike a full club that tries to pay the band in exposure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my band that AI saving an hour on invoices is welcome. We still need to rehearse the set and load the amps before a show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have four months of expenses saved and the teaching studio has a steady list, so I am not bracing for an immediate loss. A weak month of club dates is ordinary in this work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep Monday guitar pupils and the band’s Thursday rehearsal. I already use AI every day to draft set lists, and I will keep checking them against what our singer can actually sing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture. The rent is covered by lessons, and a simpler invoice lets me get home earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened in your last slow month of club work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last quiet club month cost me two paid nights, but none of my lesson pupils left. I would still ask the bar owner for autumn dates before buying new gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach a younger musician?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show my younger guitarist how to carry an amp and how to send a clear bill. Carrying amps and sending clear bills get a musician asked back.

say: I would tell the **band** that faster invoices are useful.
I would say **rehearsal and load-in** still belong to us.
think: My **four-month cushion** and steady pupils cover an ordinary quiet club month.
I will not buy **new gear** until more dates are booked.
do: Keep **Monday guitar lessons** and Thursday band rehearsals.
Check my existing **AI set lists** against our singer’s range.
feel: I feel **calm** because lessons cover rent and work stays familiar.
S0.quote: Carrying amps and sending clear bills get a musician asked back.
fieldNote: He has a **steady teaching list** and enough savings for a typical slow club month.
His daily **AI use** is already part of work, so no new learning action is claimed.

steps.text: Keep Monday guitar lessons and Thursday band rehearsals
Wait for booked autumn club dates before buying gear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the club owner that AI can handle posters, booking and demo tracks, but a live band should still get the agreed fee. I would ask for the full amount in writing before we unload.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the demo loops I sell to other acts to dry up, maybe one sixth of my good-month income. My teaching studio is steadier, but a few pupils may think a screen is enough for beginners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would test a paid Saturday beginner guitar group, but only if the studio has six prepaid places. During the first year I would use AI to prepare practice tracks for that group, listen through each track, and keep private pupils alongside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about demo work, but I can test another product while I have savings. I do not want to gamble studio rent on empty chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many students make Saturday worth opening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six places at 15 cover the extra room time and leave a fee. With three, I will cancel the group and teach the private slots instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you trust those AI tracks with pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI daily for rough tracks already. I would only send the new practice tracks after checking that the tempo suits a beginner and the licence lets me share them.

say: I would ask for a **written live fee** before the band unloads.
I would tell parents that **beginner lessons** still need a person listening.
think: My **demo loops** may lose buyers, cutting a good month by around one sixth.
Some **beginners** may leave lessons for a screen.
do: Test a **Saturday guitar group** next month with six prepaid places.
Send **AI practice tracks** only after listening and checking sharing rights.
feel: I feel **anxious** about demo income but able to try a paid class.
S1.quote: I do not want to gamble studio rent on empty chairs.
fieldNote: He sets a **six-prepaid-place threshold** before adding a Saturday group at the studio.
He already uses AI but conditions **shared tracks** on tempo and licence checks.

steps.text: Run a Saturday guitar group only with six prepaid places
Send checked AI practice tracks if sharing rights allow
Keep private guitar lessons alongside the Saturday group

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that AGI by 2028 could make every demo we sell, but I would still demand a live fee. We should book our own shows rather than wait for a club to discover us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the demo loops vanish in 2028 and some pupils may cancel. Robots that can do stage work arrive around 2031, so the band has three more years, but the lost demos leave a hole immediately.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask the community hall for a price on one ticketed show and check whether the band can cover the deposit. If 2028 AGI removes demo sales, I would run that show only after enough tickets are paid to cover hall and player fees, and I would cut sample subscriptions first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, not helpless. Four months saved gives me time to test a show. I cannot spend four months of savings on a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What cost would you cut if demo buyers leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The subscriptions are 45 a month. I would cancel them if no client buys my samples, not while they still pay for themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your family help with the show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My brother can lend a van for the show if he is free that night. I would not ask him to pay for the hall or make the band work for nothing.

say: I would ask the band to seek **ticketed shows** with a clear live fee.
I would tell clubs that **AGI demos** do not make unpaid stage work fair.
think: My **demo sales** could vanish in 2028, before stage robots around 2031.
Four months saved buys time, but **empty tickets** could consume it.
do: Price one **community hall show** this week and check the deposit.
Run the **ticketed show** after 2028 only if AGI ends demos and prepaid tickets cover hall and players.
Cancel **45 monthly subscriptions** if demo buyers leave; borrow my brother’s van only when available.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost demos, though I have a funded test.
S2.quote: I cannot spend four months of savings on a guess.
fieldNote: He separates **2028 demo loss** from a possible 2031 robot effect on stage work.
His ticket condition protects **player pay** and savings before a show is booked.

steps.text: Run show in first year after 2028 if demos end and tickets cover hall and players
Cancel 45 monthly sample subscriptions if demo buyers leave
Borrow his brother’s van if available for the show

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my pupils that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to learn how to play together and book our own rooms. I would ask the hall to offer a regular paid band night if our trial show sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The demo loops may go in 2031, but five years is enough to build direct ticket buyers. Robots around 2034 could play a stage set; I do not know if people would pay to see that rather than neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would run one hall show this winter only if advance tickets pay the deposit and players. If it sells, I would collect email addresses with consent and book a second night next season; after 2031 I would keep the paid lessons and compare the show profit with old demo fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy. A promising hall date is not a wage until tickets sell. Five years helps me build the list without betting the studio on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What ticket number would justify another hall night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would aim for 60 paid tickets before a second date. If we get 30, I would keep our club dates and avoid signing a hall contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would AI contact the audience for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not have AI send messages pretending to be me. I can use it to draft, then call the people who actually came to hear us.

say: I would ask for a **regular paid night** if the trial show sells.
I would tell pupils to build a **real audience** over five years.
think: The **demo market** may vanish in 2031, but direct ticket buyers might replace it.
I cannot predict whether **2034 stage robots** would draw an audience.
do: Run one **hall show** this winter if advance tickets cover costs.
Book a **second date** only after 60 paid tickets and consent-based contacts.
feel: I feel **uneasy** until ticket money actually arrives.
S3.quote: A promising hall date is not a wage until tickets sell.
fieldNote: His **60-ticket gate** stops a single hopeful show becoming a recurring liability.
He uses AI for **drafts**, but insists audience contact must be honest and consensual.

steps.text: Run a hall show this winter if advance tickets pay deposit and players
Keep paid guitar lessons after 2031 AGI arrives
Book a second hall night after 60 paid tickets and consented audience contacts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to own a small audience rather than chase demos. I would encourage apprentices to learn sound checks as well as solos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the hall nights work, by 2036 I might have enough repeat buyers to live without demo sales. Stage robots around 2039 could copy our set, but I cannot know what friends will pay to hear together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I would save a third of each profitable hall night after paying players and hall rent. In the first year after 2036 I would compare paid attendance with the last three seasons and keep the studio lessons unless a better income is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the long-term stage question, though four months saved and steady pupils keep the next few years secure. I would not lose sleep over a robot that is thirteen years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an apprenticeship look like on a paid night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would teach one younger player the load-in and sound check at a paid gig if the venue agrees. I would pay that player from the show fee, not call unpaid work training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know a hall show was profitable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A good night is one that pays everybody and leaves something to save. A full room that leaves the drummer unpaid is a bad night.

say: I would tell the band to build **repeat buyers** over the decade.
I would teach apprentices **sound checks** on paid shows.
think: Profitable **hall nights** might replace demo sales before 2036.
I cannot tell how **2039 robots** would change live audiences.
do: Save a **third of show profit** after paying players and rent.
Compare **paid attendance** after 2036 with three earlier seasons.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about distant stage work, while current pupils and savings protect me.
S4.quote: A full room that leaves the drummer unpaid is a bad night.
fieldNote: He defines **profit** only after hall costs and every player’s fee are covered.
His apprenticeship plan includes **paid gigs**, venue consent and practical stage work.

steps.text: Save one third of hall profit after paying players and rent
Keep studio guitar lessons after 2036 unless another income is real

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because demo buyers could leave before our own shows sell. Affordable hall dates, paid advance tickets and clear band fees would let me test a different income without burning savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the player carrying cases at midnight. The person loading the van is part of the music business too.

headlineQuote: The person loading the van is part of the music business too.
portrait: At **27**, Karl teaches guitar, sells demos and leads a band with a music master’s and four months saved.
He uses **AI daily** for draft tracks and set lists, checking range, tempo and sharing rights before use.
His **traditional outlook** favours paid work, honest ticket sales and apprentices learning on paid gigs.
He tests **hall shows** only when advance sales cover players and room costs, then saves real profit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove Karl’s demo buyers before ticketed hall shows replace their fees.
whatWouldHelp: **Affordable hall dates**, advance ticket sales and clear band fees would let Karl test a different income.
